title: Father to Son (Poem, Hornbill)
tagline: Elizabeth Jennings’ plea from a father who lives with his son and does not know him.

overview.intro: A father speaks about a son who shares his house yet not his life: they occupy the same rooms, sleep under the same rules, and have built a wall of silence between them. The unit follows the poem from its statement of estrangement, through the father’s memory of his own childhood and his attempts at speech, to the closing lines in which both reach out, longing for something to forgive — a plea for recognition rather than an accusation.

learningOutcomes: Summarise the father’s complaint and his self-examination.
Explain the significance of the wall of silence.
Account for the poem’s final lines about forgiveness.
Analyse how the poem gives the son no voice and why that matters.
Answer extract questions on voice and theme.

blocks.text: The poem opens on an intimacy that has failed: the father and son live together and have done so long enough to have shared every ordinary circumstance, yet the father describes them as people from separate worlds who cannot understand one another. The estrangement is not a quarrel — nothing in the poem has been shouted — but a slow accretion of silence, and the father reports it with a mixture of bewilderment and guilt that shapes the whole poem: he does not know how the distance arose and he is aware that part of it is his.

The imagery of the wall is central. The father says they have built a wall of silence — built, not found, which assigns responsibility jointly, and silent rather than violent, which describes a failure of speech rather than an argument. Crucially the father cannot see over it: his complaint is that he does not know his son’s tastes, thoughts or company, and the poem keeps returning to that ignorance as the injury he most regrets. The reader is given only the father’s side, and that limitation is deliberate — the son’s silence in the poem mirrors his silence at home.

items: They live together yet behave like strangers from different worlds.
The distance is a slow accretion, not a single quarrelsome event.
The wall of silence is built by both, and the father admits his share.
The father cannot see over it: he does not know his son.
The son never speaks in the poem — his silence is structural.

learn.title: The father’s memory and his attempts at speech

blocks.text: Two counterweights appear in the middle of the poem. The first is memory: the father recalls his own childhood and the way he, too, was once misunderstood or unheard, and the recollection softens his complaint into recognition — he has been on the other side of the wall. The second is his attempts to speak, which he reports as failures: he has tried to explain, to ask, to offer his experience, and has met either a short answer or none at all. The poem treats these attempts with honesty — they are well meant and slightly clumsy, which is precisely the condition of most such conversations.

What the father wants is small and enormous at once: to know what his son likes, to be told something, to be allowed into ordinary daily detail. The poem makes clear that he is not asking for agreement or obedience — he has stopped expecting those — but for information about a person he loves. This matters for the ending: a plea for detail rather than control is what makes his eventual recognition, that forgiveness may be what they both need, credible rather than self-serving.

blocks.caption: What the father has and has not got
rows: A shared house and daily proximity
Knowledge of his son’s tastes and thoughts
Conversation that continues past a sentence
A way to use that memory without lecturing
Any response that tells him it is received

blocks.text: The close turns the poem from complaint into appeal. The father speaks of releasing the son, of making room, and of accepting whatever the son brings — and the final image is of two people reaching out towards each other, each longing for something to forgive. The phrase is exact and easily misread: he does not claim the son has wronged him, nor he the son. What each wants is the ordinary human permission that forgiveness grants — to resume a relationship without an accounting of who was silent first.

That ending redefines the poem’s problem. Throughout, the father has described a wall; at the close he offers to take it down on his side, and the wall becomes neither party’s fault once both are shown reaching. The generosity of the gesture is reinforced by what precedes it: he does not demand an explanation for the years of silence, he asks only for the chance to give and receive forgiveness as a form of greeting. Answers on the ending should quote the final line exactly, distinguish forgiveness from excuse, and note that the son remains silent even here — the reader must infer his reaching from the father’s certainty that it exists.

items.text: The wall of silence they have built.
items.note: Joint responsibility stated in one image: built, not imposed.
Forgiveness offered as a greeting rather than as a verdict.

learn.title: Voice, absence and the poem’s restraint

blocks.text: The poem is a monologue in which the absent party is the subject, and its technique depends on that asymmetry. The son is never quoted, never characterised except through the father’s ignorance, and never accused — the father’s attempts to describe him dissolve into admission that he cannot. The effect is to make the reader supply the son’s side: we imagine a boy guarded because the father’s voice, for all its warmth, has often spoken at him rather than to him.

The form reinforces the intimacy. The lines are plain and largely unmusical, the images domestic rather than decorative, and there is no display of grief — the father’s pain is reported rather than performed. That restraint is what gives the ending its force: a poem that has not dramatised its wound can credibly end in reconciliation instead of triumph. For extract answers, identify what the father says, what he admits, and what he never says about the son — the third category is where the poem’s real feeling is stored.

blocks.caption: Techniques and their effects
rows: The reader imagines the son’s side
Ends in reconciliation rather than display

questions.prompt: The father describes the distance between himself and his son as:
options: A quarrel that ended the relationship
A wall of silence they have built together
The result of the son’s cruelty
questions.answer: A wall of silence they have built together
questions.explanation: Built by both and silent rather than violent, the wall describes a failure of speech with shared responsibility.

Does not know his son’s tastes, thoughts or company
questions.answer: Does not know his son’s tastes, thoughts or company
questions.explanation: Proximity without knowledge is the injury he names: they share a house and he cannot see over the wall.

Each wants the permission to resume a relationship without accounting for the silence
questions.answer: Each wants the permission to resume a relationship without accounting for the silence
questions.explanation: Forgiveness is offered as a greeting rather than demanded as a verdict: both reach, neither accuses.

questions.prompt: The father says he and his son live like strangers from different ________ .
questions.explanation: The phrase states the estrangement: shared space, separate lives.

questions.prompt: The father recalls his own ________ , which softens his complaint into recognition.
questions.explanation: Memory puts him on the other side of the wall and turns blame into understanding.

questions.prompt: What problem does the father describe in the poem?
questions.answer: The father describes a household in which he and his son live together yet know nothing of one another: they share a house, routine and roof, but behave like strangers from different worlds because they have built a wall of silence between them. He cannot see over it — he does not know what his son likes, thinks or who his company is — and his attempts at conversation are met with short answers or none. He reports the situation with bewilderment rather than anger, and admits that the wall was built by both of them.
questions.explanation: The problem must be stated as proximity without knowledge, with the shared responsibility of the wall included.

questions.prompt: How does the father’s memory of his own childhood affect his complaint?
questions.answer: His recollection of his own youth changes the complaint into recognition: he remembers being young and unheard, which puts him on the other side of the wall and shows him that the distance he now suffers from is a common condition rather than his son’s personal failing. The memory also moderates his tone — instead of demanding an explanation, he becomes aware that part of the wall is his, and he turns his attention to what he can still do rather than to what went wrong. Finally, it prepares the ending, because a man who recognises himself in the person he is complaining about is ready to reach out instead of insisting on being right.
questions.explanation: Three effects are required: identification, moderation of tone, and preparation for the closing reach.

questions.prompt: How does the poem treat the silence between the father and his son? Answer with evidence.
questions.answer: Silence is the poem’s subject, its structure and its device, and it operates on three levels. At the level of content, the father names it directly: he and his son have built a wall of silence, and everything he longs for — a taste, a thought, an opinion — is something a conversation might have supplied. The wall image makes the silence structural rather than momentary: it was built course by course, it is shared, and neither can see over it, so the silence is a condition they inhabit rather than an event they caused. At the level of structure, the silence governs the poem’s form: it is a monologue, and the absent party never speaks, is never quoted, and is characterised only through the father’s ignorance of him. The reader must therefore imagine the son’s side entirely, which is what gives the poem its tension — we hear a warm, bewildered man who has perhaps for years spoken at his son rather than to him, and we infer the guard that would answer such speech with short replies. At the level of technique, silence is what the poem refuses: nothing is dramatised, no grievance is performed, and the father’s pain is reported in plain domestic diction rather than displayed. That restraint is why the ending can move from silence into a reaching out without sounding implausible: a poem that has never raised its voice can credibly end in an offer of forgiveness. The answer should quote the wall image, note the monologue form, and explain how the son’s structural absence forces the reader to complete the picture, because the silence is doing all three jobs at once.
questions.explanation: Full marks require the three levels — content, structure and technique — with quotations, and the observation that the reader must supply the son’s side.

questions.prompt: Is the father to blame for the distance between them? Discuss with evidence.
questions.answer: The case for blame rests on what the poem lets the reader infer. The father has tried to talk but his attempts are described as clumsy and unavailing, which suggests that his conversations have been more statement than inquiry; he has rules, routine and expectations in the house, and the son answers with short replies, a behaviour people adopt when they expect to be talked at. The father himself concedes that the wall was built by both, and his admission implies awareness that the silence was maintained from his side too. Moreover, the poem’s form supports the charge: he holds the entire voice of the poem while the son has none, which mirrors a relationship in which one party has always had the words — and having had them, he did not learn to listen. The case against blame is equally textual. Nothing the father reports is cruel, his memory of his own youth shows empathy rather than blindness, and he asks only for detail rather than control, which marks him as affectionate rather than authoritarian. The distance also has no identified cause in the poem: it accumulated over years through silence rather than through any act, and the father is as bewildered by it as anyone, which is not the position of a person who caused something knowingly. The son’s own withdrawal contributes equally: he keeps answers short, and the poem gives no indication that he ever attempted the conversation either. The balanced judgement is that the question of fault is precisely what the poem outgrows — it begins by presenting a shared condition, examines the father’s part honestly, and ends by proposing forgiveness as a mutual need rather than an adjudication of blame, because a relationship that has reached the point of mutual longing cannot be repaired by establishing who built the wall first. An answer should therefore argue both sides from evidence — the father’s voice and the son’s silence both count — and conclude about what the ending asks for rather than who deserves the verdict.
questions.explanation: Full marks require both cases evidenced, attention to the poem’s form as evidence, and a judgement about why the ending declines to allocate blame.
